title: Visiting Iris Dataset with R
text:
The Iris dataset is a classic dataset by Ronald Fisher in 1936. It contains 150 observations of iris flowers from three species: Iris setosa, Iris versicolor, and Iris virginica.
Dataset is available on UCI Iris page.This dataset is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.
In this analysis, a local copy of the Iris dataset distributed with R is used. Storing the dataset within the repository ensures that the analysis can be reproduced without retrieving data from an external server.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
iris_data <- read_csv("data/iris.csv")
head(iris_data)

title: Visiting Iris Dataset with R
text:
Data Munipulation
The data are grouped by species using group_by(), after which summarise() is used to calculate the mean sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width for each species. The number of observations in each group is also calculated using n().
This operation transforms the original flower-level dataset into a species-level summary, making it easier to compare the typical physical measurements of the three iris species.

species_summary <- iris_data |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_sepal_length = mean(Sepal.Length),
    mean_sepal_width = mean(Sepal.Width),
    mean_petal_length = mean(Petal.Length),
    mean_petal_width = mean(Petal.Width),
    n = n()
  )

species_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  Species  mean_sepal_length mean_sepal_width mean_petal_length mean_petal_width
  <chr>                <dbl>            <dbl>             <dbl>            <dbl>
1 setosa                5.01             3.43              1.46            0.246
2 versico…              5.94             2.77              4.26            1.33 
3 virgini…              6.59             2.97              5.55            2.03 
# ℹ 1 more variable: n <int>


This demonstrates a second common manipulation: selecting observations according to a condition and retaining only variables relevant to the question.

large_petals <- iris_data |>
  filter(Petal.Length > 4) |>
  select(Species, Petal.Length, Petal.Width)

head(large_petals)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  Species    Petal.Length Petal.Width
  <chr>             <dbl>       <dbl>
1 versicolor          4.7         1.4
2 versicolor          4.5         1.5
3 versicolor          4.9         1.5
4 versicolor          4.6         1.5
5 versicolor          4.5         1.3
6 versicolor          4.7         1.6


As shown in Figure 1, petal length and petal width have a clear positive relationship. The three species also form distinct groups based on these two measurements. Iris setosa has substantially smaller petals than the other two species, while Iris versicolor and Iris virginica have larger petals with some overlap between their distributions.
The visualization therefore suggests that petal measurements contain useful information for distinguishing among the three iris species.

ggplot(
  iris_data,
  aes(
    x = Petal.Length,
    y = Petal.Width,
    colour = Species
  )
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Petal Measurements by Iris Species",
    x = "Petal length (cm)",
    y = "Petal width (cm)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Petal length versus petal width for the three iris species.

Finally, the observations are grouped by wine class and summarized using the mean of each selected chemical measurement. We also count the number of observations belonging to each class. This transforms the sample-level data into a class-level summary and allows the chemical characteristics of the three wine classes to be compared more easily.

class_summary = (
    wine_selected
    .groupby("class")
    .agg(
        mean_alcohol=("alcohol", "mean"),
        mean_malic_acid=("malic_acid", "mean"),
        mean_magnesium=("magnesium", "mean"),
        mean_color_intensity=("color_intensity", "mean"),
        n=("class", "size")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

Finally, we create a scatter plot that compares alcohol content and color intensity for the three wine classes. Each point represents one sample, while the different colour groups represent the wine classes.
The plot shows that the three classes occupy three different regions. In particular, some classes tend to have different combinations of alcohol content and color intensity. However, there is also overlap between the groups.

for wine_class, group in wine_selected.groupby("class"):
    plt.scatter(
        group["alcohol"],
        group["color_intensity"],
        label=wine_class,
        alpha=0.7
    )
plt.xlabel("Alcohol")
plt.ylabel("Color intensity")
plt.title("Alcohol vs. Color Intensity by Wine Class")
plt.legend(title="Wine class")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Alcohol content versus color intensity by wine class.
